ch5_ex2_q1a: Bounds check: the hypotenuse is longer than the longest leg (6.3) but shorter than the two legs added together ($4.7 + 6.3 = 11$). 7.86 fits.
ch5_ex2_q1b: Estimate with round numbers: $\sqrt{20^2 + 27^2} = \sqrt{400 + 729} = \sqrt{1129} \approx 33.6$. That is close to 33.27, so the answer is reasonable.
ch5_ex2_q1c: Quick estimate: 562 and 804 are roughly $7 \times 80$ and $10 \times 80$, so the hypotenuse is about $80\sqrt{49 + 100} = 80\sqrt{149} \approx 977$. That is close to 980.95.
ch5_ex2_q2a: Calculator technique: type the whole thing as $\sqrt{(7.4^2 + 10.3^2)}$ in one line. Never round $c^2$ before taking the square root.
ch5_ex2_q2b: Spot the ratio: 2.7 is $3 \times 0.9$, so the hypotenuse is $0.9\sqrt{1^2 + 3^2} = 0.9\sqrt{10} \approx 2.85$.
ch5_ex2_q2c: Why the hypotenuse is only a little longer than 152: when one leg is much shorter than the other, it adds only a small amount to the hypotenuse.
ch5_ex2_q3c: Watch the rounding: $u^2 = 236.3904$ and $u = 15.37499...$, which is just below the halfway point. Use the full calculator value, which gives 15.37, not 15.38.
ch5_ex2_q4a: Scale to whole numbers: multiply every side by 100 to get 28 and 67, find $\sqrt{67^2 - 28^2} \approx 60.9$, then divide by 100 to get 0.61. Similar triangles keep the same shape.
ch5_ex2_q4b: Take out the common factor 10: $w = 10\sqrt{287^2 - 192^2}$. Smaller numbers mean fewer keying errors.
Estimate: $2870^2 - 1920^2 = 950 \times 4790 \approx 4.55$ million, and $\sqrt{4.55 \text{ million}}$ is a bit over 2100.
ch5_ex2_q5: Shortcut: $34^2 - 25^2 = (34-25)(34+25) = 9 \times 59 = 531$, so the width is $\sqrt{531} \approx 23.04$ cm.
ch5_ex2_q6: Take out the common factor: sides 4 and 12 are $4 \times 1$ and $4 \times 3$, so the hypotenuse is $4\sqrt{1 + 9} = 4\sqrt{10} \approx 12.65$ cm.
ch5_ex2_q7a: Memorise $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$: the diagonal of a 10 cm square is $10 \times 1.414 = 14.14$ cm, with no squaring needed.
ch5_ex2_q7b: Using diagonal $= s\sqrt{2}$: $17 \times 1.414 \approx 24.04$ cm. This works for every square, so you only need one multiplication.
ch5_ex2_q7c: Mental check: $3.2 \times 1.4 = 4.48$, so a diagonal a little over 4.5 is right.
ch5_ex2_q8b: Calculator technique: store $\sqrt{90^2 - 50^2}$ in memory (for example STO A) and reuse it for both the perimeter and the area.
ch5_ex2_q8c: Exact form: area $= 50 \times 10\sqrt{56} = 500\sqrt{56} = 1000\sqrt{14} \approx 3741.66$ cm$^2$. Keeping the surd avoids rounding errors.
ch5_ex2_q9a: Pattern: legs $x$ and $kx$ give hypotenuse $x\sqrt{1 + k^2}$. Here $x\sqrt{17} = 25$, so $x = \frac{25}{\sqrt{17}} \approx 6.06$.
ch5_ex2_q9b: In a right-angled isosceles triangle, hypotenuse $=$ leg $\times \sqrt{2}$. So $3x\sqrt{2} = 18$ gives $x = \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} = 3\sqrt{2} \approx 4.24$.
ch5_ex2_q9c: Factor out $2x$: the legs are $2x \times 1$ and $2x \times 3$, so the hypotenuse is $2x\sqrt{10} = 30$, giving $x = \frac{15}{\sqrt{10}} \approx 4.74$.
ch5_ex2_q10: Why halve the base: the height of an isosceles triangle meets the base at its midpoint, splitting it into two identical right-angled triangles with legs 12.5 and 8.
ch5_ex2_q11: Formula worth remembering: an equilateral triangle of side $s$ has height $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s$. So $9\sqrt{3} \approx 15.59$ cm.
The right-angled half has sides in the ratio $1 : \sqrt{3} : 2$. That is the same triangle that gives the exact values of $\sin 30^\circ$ and $\sin 60^\circ$.
ch5_ex2_q13: Shortcut formula: the area of an equilateral triangle of side $s$ is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^2$. Here $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 84^2 = 1764\sqrt{3} \approx 3055.34$ cm$^2$.
ch5_ex2_q14: 5, 12, 13 is a Pythagorean triple, so each wire is exactly 13 m with no calculator. Learn 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and 7-24-25.
ch5_ex2_q15: The shortest way back is always the straight line (the hypotenuse), and it is always shorter than the 5.9 km already paddled. 4.34 km passes that check.
ch5_ex2_q16: Square diagonal $= s\sqrt{2}$: $27 \times 1.414 \approx 38.2$ m. Any time two points are opposite corners of a square, think $\sqrt{2}$.
ch5_ex2_q17: Converting to the smaller unit (mm) avoids decimals: $\sqrt{56^2 + 29^2} = \sqrt{3977}$. Check: $63^2 = 3969$, so the answer is just above 63.
ch5_ex2_q18a: Divide every length by the common factor 8: $24 \to 3$ and $40 \to 5$, so the missing side is $4 \times 8 = 32$. Scaling down first is often faster.
ch5_ex2_q19: A 2 : 1 rectangle has diagonal $w\sqrt{5}$: $25\sqrt{5} \approx 55.9$ m. Estimate $1500 \div 56 \approx 27$ to check.
ch5_ex2_q20: Work in hundreds: $2900 = 29 \times 100$ and $3700 = 37 \times 100$, so the distance is $100\sqrt{29^2 + 37^2} = 100\sqrt{2210} \approx 4701.06$ m.
ch5_ex2_q22a: Last-digit check: $56^2$ ends in 6 and $33^2$ ends in 9, so the sum ends in 5. $65^2$ ends in 5 but $60^2$ ends in 0, so 65 must be the answer.
ch5_ex2_q22b: Divide by the common factor 5: 60 and 175 become 12 and 35. 12-35-37 is a Pythagorean triple, so the hypotenuse is $37 \times 5 = 185$.
ch5_ex2_q22c: Last-digit check: $273^2$ ends in 9 and $136^2$ ends in 6, so the sum ends in 5. $305^2$ ends in 5 but $308^2$ ends in 4, so 305 is correct.
ch5_ex2_q23: Link to algebra: solving $x^2 = 25$ on its own gives $x = \pm 5$, but a context (a length, a time, a count of objects) can rule out solutions. Always check each solution against the situation.
ch5_ex2_q24a: Why the hypotenuse is the longest side: it is opposite the right angle, which is the largest angle in the triangle. The longest side is always opposite the largest angle.
ch5_ex2_q24b: Last-digit trick: $105^2$ ends in 5 and $208^2$ ends in 4, so the sum ends in 9. $233^2$ ends in 9 but $230^2$ ends in 0, which points to 105, 208, 233.
ch5_ex2_q25b: Divide by 7 first: 21 and 28 become 3 and 4, so MP $= 5 \times 7 = 35$ cm without squaring anything.
ch5_ex2_q25c: Shortcut from similar triangles: dropping a perpendicular to the hypotenuse gives $MQ^2 = MR \times MP$, so $y = \frac{21^2}{35} = 12.6$ cm.
By symmetry SP also equals 12.6, so RS $= 35 - 2 \times 12.6 = 9.8$ cm.
ch5_ex2_q26: Triangle BDE has sides 16 and 20, which is 4, 5 times 4, so BD $= 12$ (the 3-4-5 triple).
BD is the height of the equilateral triangle, so $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}x = 12$, giving $x = \frac{24}{\sqrt{3}} = 8\sqrt{3} \approx 13.86$ cm.
ch5_ex2_q27: Scale factor first: the Sun is $147\,000\,000 \div 385\,000 \approx 382$ times farther away than the Moon, so its diameter is about 382 times the Moon's: $3474 \times 382 \approx 1.33$ million km.
This is similar triangles, not Pythagoras: both triangles share the angle at Earth, so the sides are in proportion.
